title: Are New Zealand's design rainfalls already out of date? An out-of-sample exceedance audit of HIRDS v4 (c. 2017-2026), including Auckland's 2023 floods
hypothesis: The test pools all NZ rain gauges (target at least 250) that have QC'd sub-daily records and at least 8 out-of-sample water years: ESNZ national network plus Auckland, Northland and Hawke's Bay council gauges. Out-of-sample years are the water years after each gauge's last year used to fit HIRDS v4 (c. 2017-2026). Over those years, annual-maximum 6-h rainfall exceeds the HIRDS v4 'historical' 10% AEP (10-year) depth at that location at least 1.3 times as often as the 10% AEP implies. The observed/expected ratio is estimated with a storm-event block bootstrap, and its 95% CI lower bound must exceed 1.0. H1 is rejected if the point ratio is below 1.3 or the CI includes 1.0. Secondary claims, reported but not confirmatory: the same test at 1 h and 24 h and at the 2% AEP level; the Auckland-region stratum; a sensitivity run excluding Jan-Feb 2023; and whether HIRDS v4's climate-change-adjusted depths (RCP4.5, 2031-2050) give a ratio closer to 1.
gap: HIRDS v4 (NIWA, 2018; now on ESNZ DataHub under CC BY) underpins NZ stormwater, culvert and flood design. That includes Auckland Council's Stormwater Code of Practice, which applies a climate-change uplift to HIRDS v4 depths. HIRDS v4 was fitted to records ending around 2016. Since then NZ has had record events: Westport 2021, Nelson 2022 and 2025, Auckland Anniversary 2023 (~250 mm in 24 h at Auckland Airport) and Cyclone Gabrielle. Nobody has checked whether HIRDS's stated exceedance probabilities hold up out of sample. Wright et al. (2019, GRL) did this for US design standards and found 100-year storms markedly more frequent than stated, but there is no NZ equivalent. NZ trend studies (Griffiths 2007, 2013; Harrington & Renwick 2014) use pre-2012 data, report mixed trends and do not test design values. Stone et al. (2024) treat Gabrielle as a future design storm, but nobody has asked whether today's design tables are already miscalibrated.
value_rationale: Engineers design against these tables, and the question became urgent after Auckland's 2023 floods. A calibration ratio well above 1 would be direct evidence for revising HIRDS, Auckland's design storms and the national climate-change uplift factors. A ratio near 1 would also be useful: it would show that the 2023 events are consistent with stationary design values plus bad luck. The score stays below 8 because a ~9-year window has limited power at rare AEPs.
cost_rationale: Data are small: a few GB of gauge time series plus HIRDS point tables. Computation is annual maxima, bootstrap counts and GEV refits, a few CPU-hours with no GPU. Most of the effort goes into harvesting from several portals (ESNZ DataHub API, Auckland Council WebPortal, Hilltop servers) and quality-controlling recent, partly unaudited data. That makes it days rather than hours.

datasets.name: ESNZ (ex-NIWA) DataHub: HIRDS v4 point tables and gridded depth-duration-frequency data, plus national rain-gauge time series (CliFlo successor)
datasets.access: Free DataHub account plus an online statement of purpose; HIRDS data CC BY 4.0. If the purpose check is not automatic, fall back to an in-house regional GEV fitted to pre-2017 data (see risks)
datasets.size: HIRDS point tables <50 MB; gridded HIRDS ~1 GB; hourly/10-min rainfall for ~300 gauges ~1-2 GB

datasets.name: Auckland Council Environment Auckland data portal (Aquarius WebPortal): ~100+ Auckland rain gauges, many 1-5 min tipping-bucket records
datasets.access: No account; click-through terms of use (cite Auckland Council; raw data may not be redistributed, derived results may be published)

datasets.name: Northland Regional Council Hilltop server (rainfall, 253 site listings; e.g. site 104977 runs 2010-2026 at sub-hourly resolution)
Hawke's Bay Regional Council Hilltop server (rainfall, 235 site listings; covers Gabrielle)

lit_for: Wright, Bosma & López-Cantú 2019 (GRL, doi:10.1029/2019GL083235): regional aggregation shows US '100-year' storms have become more frequent than design standards assume. This is the direct template, with no NZ counterpart
Stone et al. 2024 (Earth's Future, doi:10.1029/2024EF004772): historical warming raised Gabrielle-like regional totals by ~10% and peak rates by ~20%
Aldridge & Bell 2024 (Environ. Res.: Climate, doi:10.1088/2752-5295/ada1f0): NZ review expecting the largest increases in short-duration extremes, so the 1-6 h durations deserve priority
Brook & Nicoll 2024 (Landslides, doi:10.1007/s10346-024-02258-0): the 27 Jan 2023 Auckland storm (265 mm in a day, ~1-in-200-yr estimate) shows how impactful out-of-sample events are
lit_against: Griffiths 2007 and 2013 (Weather and Climate) and Harrington & Renwick 2014: NZ daily rainfall extremes show weak or mixed trends to ~2011, so a large shift since 2016 would be surprising

Serinaldi & Kilsby 2015 (Adv. Water Resour., 'Stationarity is undead'): sampling uncertainty usually swamps apparent non-stationarity in short windows, so an exceedance excess may not be distinguishable from noise

Vesuviano et al. 2021 (J. Flood Risk Manag., doi:10.1111/jfr3.12703): recalibrating depth-duration-frequency models moves return-period estimates substantially, so model choice rather than climate could drive any mismatch
Spatial clustering: a few storms (Gabrielle, Jan 2023) may contribute most exceedances, leaving few effective independent events and wide CIs
method: Harvest sub-daily rainfall for all gauges with at least 8 out-of-sample years. Keep only QC'd data (portal quality codes) and complete water years (July-June, at least 90% coverage). Compute sliding-window annual maxima for 1, 2, 6, 12, 24 and 72 h. Read HIRDS v4 historical depths at each gauge's coordinates by log-linear interpolation across AEPs. For each duration and AEP, count observed exceedances and compare with the expected count (AEP x station-years) as an O/E ratio. Get CIs from a storm-event block bootstrap that resamples dates on which any gauge exceeded, which preserves spatial dependence; cross-check with a Poisson model with storm random effects. As a sanity control, compute the same ratio for in-sample years, where it should be about 1. Secondary analyses: an Auckland stratum, excluding 2023, HIRDS RCP-adjusted depths, and a regional GEV refit with and without post-2016 years to quantify the update to 1% AEP depths.
plan: Confirm the HIRDS v4 fitting period and per-gauge record end from the v4 technical report. Freeze the out-of-sample window and preregister H1 with its duration, AEP and 1.3 threshold

Register a free ESNZ DataHub account and download HIRDS v4 historical and RCP-adjusted depth tables for all candidate gauge locations. If access stalls, switch to the preregistered in-house regional-GEV baseline

Harvest sub-daily rainfall from DataHub, the Auckland Council WebPortal (click-through) and the Northland and Hawke's Bay Hilltop APIs. Harmonise time zones and units and apply quality-code filters and completeness rules
Compute sliding-window annual maxima per water year and duration, and log gauge metadata (record length, distance to the nearest HIRDS gauge)
Compute O/E exceedance ratios with storm-event block-bootstrap CIs, and the in-sample control ratios
Run secondary and sensitivity analyses: Auckland stratum, excluding Jan-Feb 2023, RCP-adjusted HIRDS, 1-h/24-h and 2% AEP, and daily-only gauges with a fixed-interval correction
Refit regional GEVs including post-2016 years and report how much 1% and 2% AEP depths change for Auckland and nationally
Write up with maps of gauge-level ratios and a plain-language note for stormwater designers
risks: Access: DataHub needs a free account and a stated purpose. If that turns into manual approval, HIRDS becomes out of reach, and the fallback baseline (an in-house regional GEV on pre-2017 data) tests 'stationary design methods' rather than HIRDS itself. If ESNZ has since released an updated HIRDS that uses post-2016 data, the audit must use archived v4 values. Selection: the lead was motivated by Auckland 2023, which is why the confirmatory test is national and has a no-2023 sensitivity. Recent council data may be provisional, and gauge network changes may bias coverage toward wetter, newer sites. Fewer qualifying gauges than the target would widen the CIs. Power is low at 2% AEP. No Māori data are involved.
plain_summary: Engineers size Auckland's pipes, culverts and stormwater ponds from national 'design rainfall' tables that say how often big downpours should happen. This study checks whether, since those tables were built around 2016, downpours meant to come once a decade have actually been happening more often across NZ, Auckland's 2023 floods included. If they have, the tables and the infrastructure built to them need updating.
local_relevance: Auckland Council Healthy Waters, Auckland Transport and Watercare designers, ESNZ as HIRDS custodian, and national design guidance (MfE, NZ Transport Agency) would learn whether current design storms and their climate uplifts are already being exceeded too often. They would also get a quantified update to Auckland's 1% AEP depths.

title: A hydrological noise floor for volcanic-unrest detection under Auckland: 13 years of ambient-noise seismic velocity monitoring across the Auckland Volcanic Field
hypothesis: Daily relative seismic velocity changes (dv/v, 0.5-2 Hz coda) are measured from ambient-noise cross-correlations between GeoNet Auckland Volcanic Field stations, 2013-2026. They are predominantly hydrological. A rainfall-driven pore-pressure-diffusion model plus a seasonal thermoelastic term, fitted on 2013-2020 only, explains at least 50% of the variance of 30-day-smoothed dv/v in the held-out 2021-2026 period: median R^2 >= 0.5 across station pairs with mean coherence >= 0.5. The held-out period includes the record-wet January-February 2023. H1 fails if median held-out R^2 < 0.5. Secondary claims: the post-correction residual 2-sigma noise floor is <= 0.05%, the size of the precursory decreases reported at Piton de la Fournaise; and dv/v shows no step greater than 2 sigma at the March 2020 COVID lockdown, which tests robustness to changes in noise sources.
gap: Auckland is built on a monogenetic basaltic field (~53 centres; last eruption ~500 yr BP). Unrest detection relies on seismicity and GNSS. O'Hagan et al. (2026) just produced the first self-consistent ML catalogue of AVF seismicity (~21 events/yr above M0.6), but no continuous velocity-change monitoring exists. Ambient-noise dv/v is a standard precursor tool elsewhere (Brenguier et al. 2008), but it is strongly driven by rainfall and groundwater (Sens-Schönfelder & Wegler 2006; Clements & Denolle 2018). Its noise floor in an urban, groundwater-rich volcanic field is unknown. Earlier AVF ambient-noise work imaged static structure (Ensing et al. 2017) or measured noise levels during the 2020 lockdown (van Wijk et al. 2021), not velocity change. Auckland's record 2023 rainfall gives a natural experiment for the hydrological response, and the lockdown gives a control for changes in noise sources.
value_rationale: This is a new, continuous monitoring observable for NZ's highest-consequence volcanic setting, with a quantified false-alarm baseline. It tells GeoNet whether dv/v could detect magma-ascent-scale changes beneath Auckland at all. It scores mid-range because it calibrates a tool rather than detecting unrest, and dv/v-hydrology coupling is well known elsewhere; the novelty is the AVF application and the noise floor.
cost_rationale: GeoNet day files are ~7-12 MB per channel-day at 100 Hz. Z components for ~8-11 stations from 2013-2026, plus horizontals at 3-4 stations for single-station cross-components, come to ~0.6-0.9 TB transferred. This is streamed from AWS (download, decimate, correlate, delete), so at most ~20 GB of correlations and metadata are kept. Cross-correlation and stretching with NoisePy, MSNoise or SeisMIC take a few CPU-days on 32 cores, with no GPU. Most of the wall time is network-bound transfer.

datasets.name: GeoNet continuous waveforms, AWS open-data bucket (AVF stations ABAZ, AWAZ, EPAZ, ETAZ, HBAZ, KBAZ, MBAZ, MKAZ, RVAZ, WIAZ, WTAZ; EH*/HH* at 100 Hz; checked available for 2013, 2019 and 2026)
datasets.size: ~7-12 MB per channel-day; ~0.6-0.9 TB for the planned subset, streamed rather than stored

datasets.name: GeoNet FDSN station metadata (instrument epochs and responses; several AVF sites changed location codes and sensors in 2024-2026)
O'Hagan & Chamberlain AVF earthquake and quarry-blast catalogues 2011-2022 (QuakeML), used to mask transients
Auckland Council Environment Auckland: rainfall and groundwater-level bores (validation of the hydrological driver)
datasets.access: No account; click-through terms of use (no redistribution of raw data)

datasets.name: ESNZ DataHub station rainfall (backup forcing, e.g. Auckland Airport, Whenuapai)

lit_for: Sens-Schönfelder & Wegler 2006 (GRL, doi:10.1029/2006GL027797): a rainfall/groundwater model explains seasonal dv/v at Merapi volcano, the model class used here
Clements & Denolle 2018 (GRL, doi:10.1029/2018GL077706): ambient-noise dv/v tracks groundwater levels in an urban basin (Los Angeles)
Feng et al. 2021 (JGR Solid Earth, doi:10.1029/2021JB022650): single-station cross-component dv/v resolves hydrological seasonal velocity changes, useful where inter-station coherence is weak
van Wijk et al. 2021 (Solid Earth, doi:10.5194/se-12-363-2021): AVF station noise is well characterised and dropped sharply during the 2020 lockdown, giving a natural control on noise sources
Brenguier et al. 2008 (Nat. Geosci., doi:10.1038/ngeo104): pre-eruptive velocity decreases of order 0.05% at Piton de la Fournaise, which sets the target noise floor
lit_against: O'Hagan et al. 2026 (NZJGG, doi:10.1002/jgo2.70063) and Zenodo 15825886: AVF monitoring improvements are already under way via ML seismicity catalogues. dv/v may add little if unrest would show first in seismicity

Ensing, van Wijk & Spörli 2017 (NZJGG, doi:10.1080/00288306.2017.1337643): AVF ambient-noise correlations are dominated by ocean microseism and cultural noise, so coda stability at 0.5-2 Hz over short inter-station paths may be poor
Seasonal and urban changes in noise sources can bias dv/v measured by stretching. The lockdown control may reveal source sensitivity that undermines the hydrological interpretation
Monogenetic-field precursors are poorly constrained (Sherburn et al. 2007 estimate days to weeks), so the 0.05% target is borrowed from a different volcano type
method: Stream daily miniSEED from the GeoNet AWS bucket for 8-11 AVF stations (Z, plus 3-component at 3-4 sites) for 2013-2026. Preprocess: detrend, remove response, decimate to 20 Hz, spectrally whiten over 0.3-5 Hz and apply running-absolute-mean normalisation. Mask catalogued earthquakes and quarry blasts using the GeoNet and O'Hagan catalogues. Compute daily cross-correlations for all ZZ pairs and single-station cross-components. Measure dv/v by stretching (with MWCS as a cross-check) in coda windows, against references built separately for each instrument epoch, with an offset parameter at each sensor change. Forward model: dv/v(t) = c_epoch + a*[rainfall convolved with a 1-D pore-pressure diffusion kernel (diffusivity, depth)] + seasonal temperature term + linear drift. Fit on 2013-2020 and predict 2021-2026, scoring held-out R^2 per pair; the median R^2 is the primary statistic. Validate the hydrological term against Auckland Council groundwater bores. Test for a step at the 26 Mar 2020 lockdown and estimate the residual noise floor from the 2-sigma of held-out residuals.
plan: Preregister bands, coda windows, pair-quality criteria, model form, the 2013-2020/2021-2026 split and the R^2 >= 0.5 threshold. Build an instrument-epoch table from FDSN metadata
Write a streaming pipeline (download, preprocess, correlate, delete) and benchmark throughput on one station-year. Size the transfer and drop stations with large gaps
Run correlations for all pairs and single-station cross-components for 2013-2026, keeping only daily CCFs and quality metrics
Measure dv/v (stretching plus MWCS), stitch across instrument epochs and screen pairs by coherence
Harvest rainfall and groundwater series. Fit the pore-pressure-diffusion and seasonal model on 2013-2020 and predict 2021-2026, including Jan-Feb 2023
Run confirmatory scoring (held-out R^2), then secondaries: residual noise floor, lockdown step test and the 2023 response compared with the prediction interval
Release an open, re-runnable AVF dv/v pipeline and time series for GeoNet/ESNZ, and write up
risks: Transfer volume and S3 throughput could stretch wall time. Instrument upgrades in 2024-2026 (new location codes, EH to HH sensors) can introduce artificial offsets near the end of the record. Urban noise non-stationarity and weak coda at short distances may give low coherence, so few pairs may qualify. Rainfall alone may be a poor proxy for groundwater in the AVF's fractured basalt aquifers. Te Mana Raraunga: no Māori data are used and there is no fieldwork. The AVF maunga are taonga of Ngā Mana Whenua o Tāmaki Makaurau (co-governed by the Tūpuna Maunga Authority), so hazard findings should be communicated with care and offered to the Authority and to Auckland Emergency Management alongside GeoNet.
plain_summary: Auckland sits on about 53 volcanoes. Rising magma could subtly change how fast seismic waves travel through the ground, and GeoNet's Auckland seismometers can track that continuously from the background 'hum' they record. Rain soaking into the ground also changes wave speeds, so this study measures 13 years of those changes, works out how big the rain-driven 'noise' is (including after the record-wet 2023 summer), and so how small a volcanic signal could be detected.
local_relevance: GeoNet/ESNZ volcano monitoring, the DEVORA research programme and Auckland Emergency Management could adopt the pipeline as an extra unrest indicator. They would get a published baseline that distinguishes rain-driven changes like January 2023 from anything magmatic.

title: Rarity, not depth? Impact-based rainfall thresholds for NZ flooding from eight years of Fire and Emergency callouts
hypothesis: The unit is the NZ suburb-day, July 2017 - June 2025, restricted to suburbs with an hourly rain gauge within 10 km. The outcome is at least one FENZ flood callout (NaturalDisasterType = 'Flood'). Models are trained on FY2017/18-2023/24 and tested on held-out FY2024/25. A logistic model that uses the local annual exceedance probability (from HIRDS v4) of the day's maximum 6-h rainfall achieves at least 5% lower held-out log-loss than an otherwise identical model using absolute 6-h depth. The paired bootstrap 95% CI of the difference must exclude zero, and the AEP model must also win in a majority of regions under leave-one-region-out cross-validation. H1 fails if either condition is not met. Secondary outputs: region-specific callout curves, including the AEP and depth at which callout probability first exceeds 10 times its background rate, and an Auckland curve with 27 Jan 2023 placed on it.
gap: NZ heavy-rain warnings and emergency surge planning still rely largely on fixed national rainfall-depth criteria. Yet the same 100 mm/24 h is routine on the West Coast and damaging in Auckland. Post-2023 reviews of the Auckland flood response and the North Island severe-weather events highlighted gaps in warnings and in emergency-service surge capacity. No NZ study has related rainfall to a national, time-stamped, objective impact record. FENZ's incident dataset (CC BY 4.0, 2017/18-2024/25, ~4,000 flood callouts and ~99% suburb-coded) has not been used for this. International analogues use insurance claims (Spekkers et al. 2013; Papagiannaki et al. 2022) or citizen reports (Tian et al. 2019). The UK validated return-period-based rainfall alerts (Hurford et al. 2012), but nobody has tested 'rarity versus depth' in NZ.
value_rationale: It turns an untapped open dataset into impact thresholds for each region, and Auckland's are directly relevant to warning criteria and surge planning, both actively debated since 2023. Either outcome changes practice: if rarity wins, warnings should be expressed as local AEPs (HIRDS); if depth wins, current criteria are defensible. It is not higher because callouts are an imperfect, capacity-limited impact proxy.
cost_rationale: Data are small: FENZ CSVs ~0.6 GB, gauge series ~2 GB, plus suburb polygons and HIRDS tables. Models are GLMs/GLMMs on ~10^6-10^7 suburb-days, CPU-only and hours to run. The effort is in geocoding suburb names, assembling gauges from several portals, and robustness checks.

datasets.name: Fire and Emergency New Zealand Incident Data, FY2017/18-2024/25 (one row per exposure; StartDateTime, Suburb, TLA, region, IncidentType, NaturalDisasterType). 2017/18 has 402 flood-coded rows and 2022/23 has 925; Auckland had 608 incidents on 27 Jan 2023 against a daily median of 72
LINZ NZ Suburbs and Localities (polygons for geocoding FENZ suburb/TLA strings)
datasets.access: Free LINZ Data Service account (CC BY 4.0)

datasets.name: Hourly/sub-hourly rain gauges: ESNZ DataHub national network, Auckland Council WebPortal, Northland and Hawke's Bay Hilltop servers
datasets.access: ESNZ: free DataHub account. Auckland Council: click-through terms (https://environmentauckland.org.nz/Data). NRC/HBRC Hilltop: open, no account

datasets.name: HIRDS v4 depth-duration-frequency tables at gauge locations (to convert depth to local AEP)
datasets.access: Free ESNZ DataHub account plus online purpose statement (CC BY 4.0)

datasets.name: Stats NZ Statistical Area 2 boundaries and 2023 Census usually-resident population (exposure offset)
datasets.access: Free Stats NZ Datafinder account (CC BY 4.0)

lit_for: Spekkers et al. 2013 (HESS, doi:10.5194/hess-17-913-2013): rainfall-related insurance claims rise sharply with intensity, so objective impact records support thresholds
Papagiannaki et al. 2022 (Water, doi:10.3390/w14060994): damage-triggering rainfall thresholds derived from claims vary across a region, consistent with local adaptation
Tian et al. 2019 (Sci. Total Environ., doi:10.1016/j.scitotenv.2019.06.355): critical rainfall thresholds for urban pluvial flooding can be inferred from citizen reports

Hurford et al. 2012 (J. Flood Risk Manag., doi:10.1111/j.1753-318X.2012.01133.x): UK Extreme Rainfall Alerts use return-period thresholds, and their validation shows that rarity-based criteria are operationally viable
lit_against: Within a region, local AEP and absolute depth are almost collinear. Identification therefore rests on between-region contrasts dominated by a few big events (Jan 2023, Gabrielle), which may make the test underpowered or event-driven
Spekkers et al. 2013 also found weak and noisy rainfall-claim relations at moderate intensities, where drainage condition and exposure dominate

FENZ callouts are capacity-limited and coding-dependent: on 27 Jan 2023 many calls could not be attended, and 'Special Service' or 'Assist Public' rows may hide flood jobs. The impact proxy is therefore censored at the extremes
Point gauges up to 10 km away can miss convective cells. Wright et al. 2019-style non-stationarity also implies the HIRDS AEPs themselves may be biased (see the companion HIRDS audit)
method: Parse all eight FENZ files. Define flood callouts primarily as NaturalDisasterType = Flood, with sensitivity variants adding NAT1-3 ICAD codes and water-related 'Special Service' rows. Geocode Suburb plus TLA to LINZ polygons by exact match, then fuzzy match, and report the match rate. Build a suburb-day panel. Assign rainfall from the nearest QC'd hourly gauge within 10 km (inverse-distance mean of up to 3 gauges as a sensitivity), giving the day's maximum 1-, 6- and 24-h depths. Convert depth to AEP by log-interpolating the HIRDS v4 curve at the gauge. Models are logistic GLMMs with suburb and region random effects, a population offset, season and holiday terms: (a) depth splines, (b) AEP splines, (c) both. Train on FY2017/18-2023/24 and test on FY2024/25, which includes the late-June 2025 Nelson-Tasman floods; also run leave-one-region-out CV. The primary statistic is the held-out log-loss difference (a) minus (b) with a paired block bootstrap over storm days. Then derive region-specific callout curves and onset thresholds and place 27 Jan 2023 on the Auckland curve.
plan: Preregister the outcome definition, the 10 km gauge rule, the 6-h primary duration, the train/test split and the 5% log-loss criterion
Download and parse the FENZ CSVs. Audit flood-coding consistency by year and region, and geocode suburbs to LINZ polygons (target >=95% match)
Assemble hourly gauges (ESNZ, Auckland Council, NRC, HBRC, plus other open council Hilltop servers), QC them, and compute daily maximum 1/6/24-h depths
Attach HIRDS v4 depth-AEP curves and compute AEPs. Build the suburb-day panel with population offsets
Fit the depth, AEP and combined models on training years. Score them on FY2024/25 and in leave-one-region-out CV with bootstrap CIs
Run sensitivities (outcome definitions, gauge distance, 1-h/24-h durations, excluding Jan-Feb 2023, capacity-censoring checks) and derive regional callout curves
Write up with an Auckland-focused threshold table for emergency managers and an open notebook
risks: FENZ capacity saturation and coding drift. Suburb-name geocoding errors. Gauge sparsity outside Auckland, Northland and Hawke's Bay may shrink the national sample. HIRDS access depends on DataHub's purpose statement; the fallback is AEPs from in-house regional GEV fits. Callouts reflect drainage, exposure and reporting behaviour as well as rain. Te Mana Raraunga: FENZ records include suburb-level incidents in communities with high Māori populations (Tairāwhiti, Wairoa, Northland) that are of iwi interest after Gabrielle. The study uses no ethnicity or iwi data and will not stratify by ethnicity without iwi engagement. Results will be aggregated and framed as service design, not deficit, and offered to iwi-led emergency responders (e.g. Te Rūnanganui o Ngāti Porou, Ngāti Kahungunu), consistent with the principles of rangatiratanga, manaakitanga and kaitiakitanga.
plain_summary: NZ weather warnings mostly trigger at fixed rain totals, but 100 mm of rain is routine on the West Coast and a disaster in Auckland. Using eight years of Fire and Emergency callout records, this study tests whether flood callouts track how unusual the rain is for a place rather than the raw amount. It then works out the rain level at which callouts surge in Auckland and elsewhere.
local_relevance: MetService/ESNZ (setting warning criteria), NEMA and Auckland Emergency Management (surge planning) and FENZ (pre-positioning crews) would get region-specific, impact-calibrated rainfall thresholds. Auckland would get its own callout-rainfall curve, with 27 January 2023 placed on it.
